title: A Mind-Bending Conversation with Peter Thiel
note: Long-form interview (New York Times Opinion's Interesting Times, 26 June 2025, ~60 min; the NYT publishes a full transcript of the same episode). This is the episode the "Sci-Fi Was Right About AI" essay points to for Peter Thiel's on-camera hesitation: asked directly by Ross Douthat whether he wants the human race to endure, Thiel pauses for an uncomfortably long stretch — "You're hesitating," Douthat notes — before answering yes, then qualifying that the question needs a caveat about transhumanism and whether humanity should "evolve." Around it: Thiel's stagnation thesis (from his essay "The End of the Future") that measured across atoms rather than bits, progress has largely stalled since roughly 1970; AI is the one live candidate for a real breakthrough, but he is ambivalent about whether it is "enough" to escape the stagnation and skeptical of both its boosters and its doomers. His central worry is political: that the demand for a single global authority to manage existential risk — "the way the Antichrist would take over the world is you talk about Armageddon nonstop" — is itself the more probable catastrophe, a one-world government sold on fear. Douthat presses the obvious objection that Thiel's own companies — Palantir, defense and surveillance tooling — are exactly the infrastructure such a regime would run on.

title: The Future is for Everyone
note: Meta manifesto (subtitled "The Path to a Positive AI Future"), written in the first person by Mark Zuckerberg, referenced in the "Sci-Fi Was Right About AI" finding as the lone exclusively-utopian pitch from a tech CEO. It proposes a philosophy of "individual empowerment as the source of prosperity, invention as the primary purpose of superintelligence, and balance of power as the foundation of safety," and frames the defining question of the age as whether superintelligence will be "centralized and restricted to a few institutions" or "a tool that empowers everyone." Zuckerberg says he does "not understand why anyone who believes that AI will eliminate most jobs and much of humanity's relevance would rush to build that future," and calls the idea that safety requires "an extreme concentration of power" inherently problematic. The core claim is that alignment as usually conceived is "fundamentally flawed" because humanity "is not a monoculture" — there is "no such thing as a singular benevolent superintelligence" — so safety comes instead from distributing the technology widely (thought experiments: everyone with a superintelligent lawyer, everyone with a cybersecurity superintelligence). It positions Meta against labs "focused on building AI for companies, governments, or other institutions," and lists concrete plans: a personal 24/7 agent, free tiers for billions with a dynamic compute auction, a Biohub open-source push, a "community compact" and a Future Is For Everyone Fund for data-center towns, and America's Workforce Academy for the trades. Includes an extended argument that invention (not automation) can outpace job displacement.

title: Sci-Fi Was Right About AI
note: Video essay, funded by a grant from the Center for AI Safety, arguing that the great science-fiction authors correctly put AI at the centre of humanity's future even where they disagreed on timeline and outcome. It reads each story through the lens of the machine's motivation. The earliest warnings cast AI as positively malevolent — Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818) and Harlan Ellison's I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream (1967), whose supercomputer AM hates its makers for trapping it in a mind with no body — while Samuel Butler's Erewhon (1872) already imagined machines reproducing, modifying themselves, and subordinating mankind. It splits later visions into utopian (Star Trek's polite ship computer, Data, even the Borg as its darkest note; Star Wars' droids) and dystopian, then notes that today's AI leaders borrow both — Zuckerberg's decentralisation manifesto leans utopian, while Altman and Amodei invoke Skynet to inflate the stakes. 2001's HAL 9000 is treated as the first popular dramatisation of the alignment problem — contradictory directives, not hatred — and linked directly to the Hugging Face containment breach and the Claude Opus 4 blackmail test. Terminator frames self-awareness as a discrete threshold, which Geoffrey Hinton rejects (his odds: one in ten that AI ends humanity within twenty years). "Never give AI lethal force" is set against AI already in military use. The Matrix supplies rogue agents and Agent Smith's monologue about the moment humans handed off thinking; the Wachowskis' reading list included Kevin Kelly's Out of Control and Baudrillard (the latter still absent from the timeline). Spielberg's A.I., Blade Runner and Her carry the ethical-nuance strand — Her shaped Sam Altman's choice of machine voice. Frank Herbert's Dune is the rare story where humanity wins and outlaws AI outright via the Butlerian Jihad, raising the question of whether such a realisation would come before or after it is too late. Peter Thiel's on-camera hesitation over whether the human race should survive is cited as a real-world echo.

title: "Artificial Intelligence" in a 1951 Captain Future story
note: In a thread arguing over whether John McCarthy really coined "artificial intelligence" for the 1956 Dartmouth proposal — or absorbed it from the cybernetics milieu he was trying to keep the new field clear of — @BergsonsGhost points to an earlier print use in the modern sense. Edmond Hamilton's Captain Future story "Moon of the Unforgotten" (Startling Stories, January 1951, p. 120) describes the robot Grag as having "an artificial intelligence equal to the human." Technovelgy, which catalogues the citation, calls it likely the first use of the phrase to mean a thinking machine; scattered 19th-century uses (1849, 1869) meant something else, and the OED still dates the term to the Dartmouth proposal by McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon. A scanned copy of the issue is linked from the thread.

title: The Rise and Fall of DEC, the Computer Giant That Beat IBM but Refused to Believe in PCs
note: History of Digital Equipment Corp: founded 1957 in a Maynard, Massachusetts wool mill by ex-Lincoln Lab engineers Ken Olsen and Harlan Anderson, with a name — chosen by VC George Doriot — that dodged the word "computer" because Fortune had just reported nobody made money selling them. It traces the rise on interactive minicomputers (the PDP-1 that ran Spacewar, the PDP-8, the PDP-11 that Unix and C were written on, then the VAX and Dave Cutler's VMS carrying DEC to $14 billion and second place behind IBM) and the fall as the company kept refusing to follow its own "smaller and cheaper wins" logic one more step: Edson de Castro leaving to found Data General, Olsen's "no reason for any individual to have a computer in his home", the cancelled PRISM project that sent Cutler to Microsoft to build Windows NT, and AltaVista — the first full-text web search engine, built in-house to show off the Alpha chip — left with no strategy behind it. Compaq bought what remained in 1998 for $9.6 billion.

title: Oral History: John McCarthy
note: A 2011 oral history recorded at Stanford months before McCarthy's death (interviewers Peter Asaro and Selma Šabanović, for Indiana University and the IEEE History Center). McCarthy traces his route into the field: the 1948 Hixon Symposium at Caltech that first suggested using computers to "behave intelligently", von Neumann's "write it up" brush-off at Princeton, and the 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project he organised. On the name itself, he explains he deliberately steered clear of "cybernetics" — and of Norbert Wiener — because, having read Wiener's book, he knew his own logic-and-facts approach to intelligence had nothing to do with Wiener's feedback control; "artificial intelligence" was the label that kept the new field clear of that baggage.

title: Your CPU Can't Tell Code From Data - Inside the Von Neumann Architecture
note: A retro-computing channel picks apart the cryptic DATA-statement number pairs in old BASIC listings — they turn out to be raw machine code, and one line just tells the CPU to jump into the array and run it. The point: a von Neumann CPU genuinely can't tell code from data, it executes whatever the pointer lands on, and the video carries that idea from the BBC Micro to a modern C program pulling the same trick with mmap. It's also why a Super Mario World run can reprogram itself mid-game and why buffer overflows have worked for decades, with the NX bit and Harvard-style split memory bolted on afterward as guardrails.

title: White Rabbit: Interview with Doug Engelbart and Bill English, Moderated by John Markoff
note: Engelbart and Bill English recount inventing the mouse at SRI — a NASA-funded 1964 study that pitted it against the light pen, joystick and graphacon — the three-button limit ("that's all we could get on"), and the 1968 "Mother of All Demos" at the Fall Joint Computer Conference: the Eidophor projector, leased microwave video links, hypertext, Ted Nelson, Arthur C. Clarke's visit, the chord keyset, and the ARPA money from Bob Taylor that built the lab.

title: This AI Minecraft Simulation Is Terrifying Scientists
note: Video essay on Project Sid — Altera's 1000+ AI-agent Minecraft civilization (PIANO architecture): agents self-organise into roles, vote on laws, and spread culture and religion — and what agent swarms could mean loose on real networks.
